# Baseline evaluation log

## Fresh distinct-whitelist Fusion protocol probe (29 October 2026)

Twenty fresh seeds, 129000–129019, generated independent legal Main Decks for
both seats and random 15-card Fusion Extra Decks. Tactical-v14 played both
seats. All **20/20** native duels reached terminal within 3,000 decisions, with
**8,590/8,590** decisions replay-verified and visibility-audited. Repeating
each seed reproduced all 8,590 ordered decisions, terminal observations, and
outcomes. The audit counted 48 hidden-field and 282 opponent-field legal
choice contexts. The report records 871 loaded native assets and 1,030
distinct source-card/action-kind pairs. This is sampled protocol coverage;
it does not certify arbitrary decks or historical rulings.

The ignored report is `.cache/goat-ai/m1_whitelist_fresh_129000_129019/report.json`
with SHA-256 `0bbd431205ce1624e360716dd6b2cf379b0e865f515108e93075b3369964abc1`.
Reproduce with:

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONPATH=src:. .venv/bin/python scripts/probe_random_decks.py \
  --native-root .cache/goat-ai \
  --output .cache/goat-ai/m1_whitelist_fresh_129000_129019 \
  --seed 129000 --seeds 20 --max-decisions 3000 --agent tactical \
  --verify-replays --distinct-opponents --random-extra --repeat-seeds \
  --count-card-actions --isolate-games
```

## Weak Flip synthetic-label correction (29 October 2026)

The existing `visible_audit_v1` and `visible_audit_v2` rule IDs automatically
preferred Set whenever a weak Flip monster was Normal Summoned with Set legal.
The [seven Magical Merchant branches](#seven-magical-merchant-set-versus-summon-branches-29-october-2026)
showed that this is not a reliable blanket preference: on one exact hidden
deal, Normal Summon won and Set lost. Those fixed-deal outcomes are not labels
either. The preference CLI now defaults to `visible_audit_no_weak_flip_v14`,
which excludes this category and retains the other v2 comparisons. The v1/v2
semantics remain available for replaying and validating old experiments.

The generator replay-verified and visibility-audited the six fresh source
replays containing the seven weak Flip flags. Its default v14 output contained
**zero preferences**; explicit v1 derivation on those same six replays would
produce seven weak Flip preferences. The ignored v14 manifest is
`.cache/goat-ai/visible_audit_no_weak_flip_v14_fresh_126000_126007/manifest.json`
with SHA-256
`b222c642d104efd92a78b70493fcef2a0634b5359c30931766ae1bf7bc0e189e`.
Direct derivation across all 64 previously audited source replays found ten
v1 comparisons (seven weak Flip, two Thunder Dragon search, one Ring target)
and three v14 comparisons (the two Thunder Dragon and one Ring target).
This removes an uncertain automatic training target; it does not establish a
new policy gain. Human review of each context and a held-out competitive
evaluation remain necessary.

## Seven idle own-only Ring activation branches (29 October 2026)

The [fresh policy review queue](replay_audit.md#fresh-policy-versus-tactical-review-queue-29-october-2026)
contains seven decisions where the selected policy activated a Set Ring of
Destruction in Main Phase 1 with only its own face-up monster targets visible.
For each exact recorded state, we reconstructed the duel from the verified
source prefix and compared the selected activation with the queue's legal
Tactical-v14 alternative: three Battle Phase transitions and four Normal
Summons. The selected v23 policy continued with its recorded v1 own-loss
inference mode; Tactical-v14 continued as the opponent. Every one of the 14
terminal branches replay-verified and passed the player-visibility audit.

**All seven pairs had the same winner:** two pairs were won by the policy
seat, and five by the Tactical seat. In each selected-activation continuation,
the policy's next target choice was one of its own monsters. The branch lengths
often differed, but a single fixed hidden deal and fixed continuation policy
cannot establish that the activation or alternative has higher expected value.
These results are offline diagnostics, not preference labels or evidence that
own-monster Ring activations are generally sound. The next useful signal is an
independent human judgment at the activation decision, followed by a held-out
complete-duel comparison of any trained change.

The ignored case reports and summary are in
`.cache/goat-ai/ring_idle_branch_sweep_126000_126007/`; the summary SHA-256 is
`0b44c9aaf0219be9c4bdd99889fad0aa7fd0372cc383ea8b8fdd32979f01e7b9`.
It records the source and checkpoint hashes, decision and action indices,
winner, and each branch-report hash. Reproduce the first pair with:

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONPATH=src:. .venv/bin/python scripts/evaluate_decision_branches.py \
  .cache/goat-ai/own_loss_review_source_126000_126007/matchup_01_seed_126004_seat_1.json \
  .cache/goat-ai/fv23_current_tactical_broader_33000_33031.pt \
  --native-root .cache/goat-ai --decision-index 394 \
  --action-index 1 --action-index 2 --max-decisions 3000 \
  --output-dir .cache/goat-ai/ring_idle_branch_first_reproduction
```

## Seven Magical Merchant Set-versus-Summon branches (29 October 2026)

The fresh four-pairing audit below flagged seven selected Normal Summons of
Magical Merchant when a Set of that same physical hand card was legal. We
reconstructed each exact source position from its verified seed and action
prefix, then continued the recorded Normal Summon and the corresponding Set
to a terminal native duel. The selected v23 checkpoint retained its recorded
v1 own-loss inference mode; Tactical-v14 remained the opponent. Both agents
received only their player-visible observations during continuation. All 14
branch trajectories reached terminal, replay-verified, and passed the
visibility audit.

On these seven fixed hidden states, Set changed a loss into a win **three**
times; Normal Summon changed a loss into a win **once**; the winner was the
same for the other **three**. The Normal-Summon-favoring case was seed 126002,
policy seat 0, zero-based decision 140. Three Sheep Tokens were on the policy's
field and the opponent had no visible monster. The recorded Normal Summon
entered Battle Phase and attacked directly with Merchant; the Set branch
skipped that attack. This first-turn difference does not by itself explain
the eventual winner, but the two full continuations ended differently. A
fresh repeat of both branches produced byte-identical trajectory hashes.

These are **single-seed, exact-full-state offline diagnostics**. They do not
estimate the expected value of Set, do not provide a legal online search
oracle, and are not training labels. In particular, this evidence argues
against automatically relabeling every weak Flip Normal Summon to Set. The
remaining context-dependent decisions stay in the human review queue. The
ignored seven-case summary
`.cache/goat-ai/weak_flip_branch_sweep_126000_126007.json` has SHA-256
`6b46ad174ed379e281e788f0f927da8240f23b24e2e14501d836f89a2dd0f7f9`;
it identifies each source replay, decision and legal-action index, branch
report hash, winner, and replay hash. Reproduce one case with:

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONPATH=src:. .venv/bin/python scripts/evaluate_decision_branches.py \
  .cache/goat-ai/own_loss_review_source_126000_126007/matchup_02_seed_126002_seat_0.json \
  .cache/goat-ai/fv23_current_tactical_broader_33000_33031.pt \
  --native-root .cache/goat-ai --decision-index 140 \
  --action-index 1 --action-index 6 --max-decisions 3000 \
  --output-dir .cache/goat-ai/weak_flip_branch_field_tokens_reproduction
```

Gravekeeper, Cas Stomphorst Flip Control versus Jae Kim Zombie, and Roberto

Seeds **126000–126007**, both policy seats, produced **64** terminal duels,

Every complete trajectory replay-verified and passed the player-visibility
audit; the recorded policy's **18,538** actions reproduced from the exact

replay identities and 19 displayed frames matched their saved hashes and

## Eight-case own-loss preference transfer (29 October 2026)

The new token-only Ring condition was offered **once in 96** policy-versus-
Tactical replayed duels across the seed-124100–124115 and varied-deck
seed-124900–124907 cohorts; that one offer was selected. This narrow event is
too rare to expect a one-case fit to move aggregate match results. A broader
read of the 64 varied-deck source duels found seven selected v12 visible-rule
preferences: four idle own-only Ring activations and three negative-visible-
trade Heavy Storm activations. The seven source duels were replay-verified and
visibility-audited when v12 preference files were generated. These are
automated hypotheses, not human approvals. The ignored manifest SHA-256 is
`f8a0e30a59e90a3eb22cd8f33527d2148d08f12e1ee53862a53e091d5812a2b1`.

A combined child used those seven preferences plus the single v13 token-only
Ring preference, all from policy-seat replays, with 64 sampled current-core
preservation decisions from four separate duels. Starting from the frozen
feature-v23 parent, `train_review_preferences.py` used 200 steps, learning
rate 0.0001, seed 1314, batch 16, and parent KL weight 1.0. Preference loss
fell from **2.718** to **0.081**; final sampled preservation KL was **0.046**.
The parent ranked the disfavored action first on **8/8** source positions;
the child ranked it first on **0/8**, ranked a preferred action first on
**7/8**, and had a positive preferred-minus-disfavored margin on **8/8**.
These are training positions, so they measure fit only. The ignored checkpoint
is `.cache/goat-ai/fv23_own_loss_8case_200step.pt` (SHA-256
`ff27225bb135f993ca3ca5defcf1fb56878895d8fc0543f88ebe1fc6f6bd1fc6`).

The first proposed evaluation decks were rejected by the strict unseen-Main-
Deck gate because all four compositions appeared in this child's training
sources. No result was produced from that rejected run. A fresh schedule used
Rhymus Goat versus Ryan Goat and Theeresak Goat versus the GOAT Format Guide
Dimension Fusion Turbo list, both seats and Deck assignments, seeds
125400–125415. Against the unchanged parent with own-loss guard v1 on both,
the child scored **55–73** over **128** complete native duels. Its paired
bootstrap 95% score interval was **34.38%–52.34%**; first-seat score was
29–35, second-seat score 26–38, and the longest duel had 1,483 decisions
below the 3,000-decision cap. All four Main Deck compositions passed the
unseen-training gate. This comparison gives **no evidence of a strength
improvement** and does not prove the child is weaker. Do not promote it.
The ignored tournament report is
`.cache/goat-ai/fv23_own_loss_8case_vs_parent_125400_125415.json`
(SHA-256 `6da161c702a549bc28a35f547cfe1659d864c78108804788945c8db669cb3964`).

The result supports the next M4 direction: obtain more independent judgments
on upstream activation choices across distinct card effects and board states,
then check both local own-card-loss frequency and full-duel outcomes on held-
out decks. More optimization steps on these eight automatic labels would
only test fit to the same narrow examples.

## Own-card losses remain a playing-strength problem (29 October 2026)

The current guard experiments have **not** established a win-rate improvement.
In the seed-124112 Ring case below, the v9 automated material labels missed
the Ring activation at decision 820. The older `visible_audit_v1` target rule
would prefer either opposing Sheep Token at decision 821 over the own Dekoichi,
but spending Ring on a zero-ATK token is still a poor trade. Treating the
target choice as the entire error would teach an incomplete lesson.

The opt-in `visible_selected_own_loss_with_idle_ring_v13` rule emits a
preference at the activation decision when the opponent controls only visible
Sheep Tokens, the actor has a face-up monster, and no visible own Ring target
could deal lethal damage. On that exact replay it compares the selected Ring
activation (legal index 7) with the offered Battle Phase and End Phase actions
(indices 8 and 9). The rule is a visible-state training hypothesis, not a
winning-move label. It leaves all prior versioned rule sets unchanged and does
not claim that either phase action wins the duel; the parent branch experiment
below found that a one-step delay can repeat the same error later.

One small fit tested whether that correction can change the learned policy.
The v13 generator replay-verified and visibility-audited the source duel and
emitted exactly one preference (manifest SHA-256
`6a6072713047bb9894a2fb281fc759565cf9169bbb54b4ae0c81f68cbed0c32a`).
Starting from the frozen v23 parent, `train_review_preferences.py` used 120
steps, learning rate 0.0001, seed 1313, four other replay-verified current-core
preservation duels (64 sampled decisions), batch 16, and parent KL weight 1.0.
The preference loss fell from **5.476** to **0.188**, while the final sampled
preservation KL was **0.041**. The ignored child checkpoint is
`.cache/goat-ai/fv23_ring_idle_v13_seed124112_120step.pt` (SHA-256
`edb23dfa07dec53e839806729b23e4648128322d7640fd01b2b7b309019890a3`).
At the **training position**, the parent ranked Ring first (legal index 7);
the child ranked normal summoning first (index 0) and Ring below the two
offered phase transitions. This demonstrates local fitting, not transfer.

The child scored **33–31** directly against its parent over **64** complete
native duels on fresh seeds 125300–125307, both seats and deck assignments,
using Christian Goat versus Ramon Beastdown and Jonathan Chaos versus Roberto
Phoenix. Both checkpoints used own-loss guard v1. All four Main Deck
compositions passed the unseen-training check; the paired-bootstrap 95% score
interval was **40.63%–62.5%**. First-seat score was 19–13 and second-seat
score was 14–18. All duels terminated before the 3,000-decision cap (maximum
1,309). This result does **not** establish a playing-strength gain. The ignored
report is `.cache/goat-ai/fv23_ring_v13_vs_parent_125300_125307.json`
(SHA-256 `f32e9c1dbc0f20c1f5fa0b0401e8a65cd699a809c3874b8a5ee9fe8e8530d883`).
An exact-state offline continuation of the recorded Ring action and the
offered Battle Phase action with the child policy produced two replay-verified,
visibility-audited terminal duels. The Battle Phase branch had **no later
same-turn Ring activation**, unlike the earlier parent continuation; both
branches still lost. The ignored branch report is
`.cache/goat-ai/ring_v13_child_branch_124112/report.json` (SHA-256
`53beacaa200244456632f3bb4fdb10a1927f1bd8032bed65774c097ea927b5f0`).
One synthetic preference is too small to promote a policy. Broader examples
of own-card loss and independently reviewed alternatives remain the next
training input.

## Ring on own Dekoichi: target information versus learned value (29 October 2026)

At seed 124112, policy seat 0, zero-based decision 820, the selected v23/v1
policy activated Set Ring of Destruction with three friendly face-up monsters
and two opposing Sheep Tokens. Its target prompt encoded each option's
relative controller explicitly: 0 for friendly, 1 for opposing. The selected
checkpoint nevertheless scored friendly Dekoichi **+0.412** versus opposing
Tokens **−0.601** and **−1.514** (raw logits), and targeted Dekoichi. The
effect closed at a **−2 non-token hand-plus-field material change** for the
acting player. This is a fixed, replay-verified decision diagnostic: the
input identifies whose card is targeted, but the learned ranking remains
poor in this state. The full context may still affect the best alternative.

An exact native branch forced either the recorded Ring activation or the
offered Battle Phase at that same decision, then continued with the same
selected policy and Tactical opponent. Both terminal trajectories replay-
verified and passed player-visibility auditing; **both lost**. In the Battle
Phase branch, the policy activated Ring later that turn and again targeted
its own Dekoichi, with the same −2 observed material change. This illustrates
why delaying one decision does not necessarily fix a repeated own-card
preference. The ignored branch report and replay files are under
`.cache/goat-ai/ring_own_dekoichi_branch_124112/`. The Battle Phase action is
a legal review candidate, not an optimal-play label or a demonstrated
win-rate gain.

The separate upstream activation review queue
`.cache/goat-ai/upstream_55_ring_dekoichi.json` (SHA-256
`a5b98a67401756e9ed39b54e50eb9299cb1569dd733fbe3b48c583397ee94e35`)
lets the reviewer choose among all ten legal actions before Ring activates.
The original combined queue's item 55 only asks for a target after activation.
`create_upstream_review.py` now offers a phase transition where the decision
has no Pass action, while leaving the reviewer free to choose another legal
action. No reviewer choice has been saved for this upstream item yet.

## Opt-in Chaos Sorcerer target-scope guard v9 (29 October 2026)

The selected v1 guard treats any opposing monster as a possible
target when deciding whether to defer an owned Chaos Sorcerer's optional
banish effect. [Chaos Sorcerer's official text](https://www.db.yugioh-card.com/yugiohdb/card_search.action?cid=5833&ope=2&request_locale=en)
requires a face-up target. If the opponent had only Set monsters, the guard
can permit activation when a friendly face-up monster is the only legal
target. Experimental v9 requires an opposing face-up monster for that effect
and leaves v1 unchanged for replay reproducibility. The
separate [BLS text](https://www.db.yugioh-card.com/yugiohdb/card_search.action?cid=5835&ope=2&request_locale=en)
allows any monster on the field, so an opposing Set monster still keeps BLS's
banish activation available. The existing target-choice filter prefers an
offered opposing target over self-banish.

The regression covers v1 and v9, both bosses, owned and borrowed sources, visible
face-up and hidden Set opponents, and a forced-action fallback. The focused
policy, guard, replay-queue, and native BLS/Chaos test selection passed 79
tests. The preexisting seed-124904 policy trajectory was re-audited with its
original v1 inference mode, reproducing all selected actions and native
decisions, and passing the visibility check.
The older 64-duel own-card baseline contained no eligible position with an
owned boss facing only opposing Set monsters, so v9 has no
measured duel-strength effect yet. It changes a narrow optional play filter,
not simulator legality or the checkpoint's learned preferences.

## Negative visible Heavy Storm trade ablation (29 October 2026)

An opt-in v8 inference variant extends the selected v1 own-loss filter at
**activation time**. It defers Heavy Storm when the number of opposing back-row
cards is no greater than the number of other friendly back-row cards it would
destroy. A Set Storm source is excluded from friendly collateral. The rule
uses only visible occupied zones; it cannot inspect an opposing Set card or
predict responses, tactical payoff, or later turns. It preserves an engine-
legal fallback and does not alter the neural checkpoint or simulator rules.

At all three previously verified negative-trade Heavy Storm decisions in the
seed-124900–124907 varied-deck audit, v8 chose a different legal action from
v1. This is a fixed-state correction of those observed cases, not a held-out
strength result or proof that its alternatives are best.

Fresh seed-125200–125207 direct play used four unseen 2005 Main Deck pairings,
both deck assignments and both policy seats. Against the same v1 checkpoint,
v8 won **65/128** games; the matched v1-versus-v1 control won **64/128**.
Against Tactical-v14 on the same schedule, both v8 and v1 won **35/128**.
The strict report comparator verified the unseen Main Decks, checkpoint,
native assets, scripts, source, seeds, and opponents. Its paired Tactical score
difference was **0**.

A second prespecified Tactical block on seed-125208–125239 used the two pairings
where the earlier Heavy Storm errors appeared, again with both deck assignments
and policy seats. V8 won **66/256** versus v1's **67/256**; the strict paired
score difference was **−0.39 percentage points**, 95% interval **−1.95 to
+0.78 points**. Three matched winners changed: one in v8's favor and two
against it, for one net win fewer. The exact changed seed-125220 Chaos/Goat
game was re-recorded under both
inference modes: all **625** v8 and **895** v1 decisions replay-verified and
passed the visibility audit. At decision 86, v1 activated Heavy Storm with four
other friendly back-row cards and two opposing back-row cards; v8 Set Spirit
Reaper instead. V1 later won and v8 lost on that fixed deal. Later play
and draws diverged, so that terminal comparison does not establish the
original Storm as strategically sound. It demonstrates the danger of treating
immediate card count as full action value.

Keep v8 experimental and v1 selected. The paired reports are ignored local
artifacts `heavy_v8_vs_v1_125200_125207.json` (SHA-256
`dcb8b24cf2ea1f1bd1c284cedfb00fdceaf0c1d7e691ac16fd2e1222d38f043a`),
`heavy_v1_control_125200_125207.json` (`a8ec4c574b6166377df3a88969218a6a9e5847f691dc7c6c855a88424d46c2a5`),
`heavy_v8_vs_tactical_125200_125207.json` (`0797b4dcab1fc8fdb6af50f30824cbd48415f33d2e96611e58f9a9c36544fe27`),

`heavy_v8_vs_tactical_125208_125239.json` (`18c02b7b4b49a6d326d0ba8bbc528a000093f0a51d4c65bc36531658ca984a32`),
and `heavy_v1_vs_tactical_125208_125239.json`

## Fresh own-card effects: resolved material versus decision value (29 October 2026)

### Same-state activation branches across the varied-deck flags

The other seven activation flags from this eight-case queue were branched at
the exact recorded native position. Each arm compared the recorded Ring or
Heavy Storm activation with an offered Battle Phase transition, then used the
same selected v23 checkpoint with v1 own-loss inference and Tactical-v14
opponent to terminal. All **14** complete branch trajectories replay-verified
and passed player-visibility checks. The recorded arm reproduced its source
duel in every case. Each paired arm had the **same winner**: seven of seven
unchanged. This small, selected set gives no evidence of a match outcome gain
from the phase choice.

In **three of the four Ring cases**, the Battle Phase arm activated Ring later
in the **same turn** (once in Battle Start, twice in Main Phase 2). This
explains why a one-decision alternative need not fix the behavior: subsequent
policy decisions can repeat the activation. None of the three Heavy Storm
Battle Phase arms activated Heavy Storm again that turn. The phase choice is
an offered legal action, not a human judgment that it was the best move. These
branches use the recorded hidden deal for offline analysis; a playing agent
receives only its legal observation. The ignored per-case reports and manifest
are under `.cache/goat-ai/own_card_broad_branches_124900_124907/`; manifest
SHA-256 `bfa675eaaff1ee4096cfe0da6756c43928539f307ccf4ddfc700d9b84c5718d9`.
The branch report now lists later same-turn activations by the policy seat of
the **same card code** after the branch decision. It does not claim the card
was the same physical copy or that the later use was necessarily wrong. All
seven branch pairs were rerun and independently replay-verified with this
field; it reproduced the three Ring and zero Heavy Storm later activations.
The updated ignored reports are under
`.cache/goat-ai/own_card_broad_branches_repeat_v2/`.
The branch tool now also accepts `--continuation-guard-version` to compare
inference variants from the same replayed prefix and forced branch action.
With v3 controlling the continuation after the Battle Phase alternative, all
**four Ring** branch duels completed without another same-code activation

### Observed material and the Delinquent Duo exception

The eight source duels in the varied-deck own-card review addition were
independently rechecked with `scripts/audit_review_material.py`. All **3,916**
decisions replay-verified against the pinned native core and passed the
player-visibility audit. Every one of the eight flagged activations reached
chain closure without another selected activation in its measurement window.
The four idle own-only Ring of Destruction cases each changed the acting
player's visible non-token hand-plus-field margin by **−2**. The three
negative-visible-trade Heavy Storm cases changed it by **−1, −3, and −3**.

The remaining case, MST chained to the AI's own Delinquent Duo, measured
**zero** net material change. The AI spent MST targeting its already
resolving Normal Spell, while Delinquent Duo still made the opponent discard.
The chain's net change therefore hides the wasted MST. A raw observed-material
reward would treat that decision as neutral; it does not compare against
passing on MST. This result reinforces using upstream activation reviews and
matched counterfactual evaluations for these cases instead of converting
chain deltas directly into supervised labels or an RL reward. The same caution
applies to monster abilities, whose costs and other chain links can change
the observed margin independently of whether their target was good.

An exact native branch at that MST decision (zero-based decision **5**, seed
**124904**, policy seat 0) compared the recorded MST chain with the offered
Pass. Both branches reconstructed the same verified prefix, then continued
with the same selected v23/v1 policy and Tactical-v14 opponent. Both complete
duels replay-verified and passed the visibility audit. At the first chain
closure, the acting player's material margin was **+0** from MST and **+1**
from Pass, relative to the shared starting state. Both full continuations
were wins for the policy seat, after **395** and **348** decisions. The one-card
immediate difference supports the local diagnosis; a single seed and shared
win do not establish a win-rate improvement. The branch tool now records this
open-chain material comparison in each arm's report, using only observations
legally visible at the decision and closure. It remains an offline exact-state
diagnostic, not a policy input or online search feature.

## Cross-review transfer check for human preferences (29 October 2026)

We used the new strict replay, seed, and Main Deck holdout gates to test
whether small batches of explicit human preferences transfer to other
decisions. The New Jersey snapshot has nine changed choices on Ryan versus
Theeresak Goat; the broader snapshot has 11 changed choices on Mary/Bryan
and Zombie/Dimension Fusion. Each preference file was read against its exact
source trajectory, which passed native replay and player-visibility audits.
The two groups were kept separate for this experiment.

The existing New Jersey nine-preference children, fit for 120 and 400 steps,
were scored on the **11 untouched broader** human choices. The selected v23
parent ranked the reviewed alternative first at 0/11; each child did so at
1/11. Their mean preferred-minus-recorded logit margins were −4.318,
−2.649, and −1.706 respectively. The 400-step update moved the score toward
the human choices without ranking more of them first.

For the reverse direction, two new children were trained **only** on the
11 broader preferences from the selected v23 checkpoint. Both used four
separate current-asset parent-policy replays from seeds 107600–107601 as
64 parent-KL preservation states, learning rate 0.0001, KL weight 0.5,
and seed 208; one used 120 steps and the other 400. The 120-step preference
loss fell 4.39494 → 1.21293 (final sampled KL 0.01023). At 400 steps it
fell 4.39494 → 0.08684 (KL 0.03461), and the child ranked the human action
first at **11/11 training decisions**. On the **nine untouched New Jersey**
choices, the parent ranked the human action first at 0/9 and both children
at only 1/9. Mean preference margins were −3.900, −2.701, and −2.223.
All four cross-group child scores passed the strict holdout gates, including
the preservation Main Decks in checkpoint provenance.

The 400-step broader-only child was then tested directly against its parent
on fresh seeds 125100–125107, Christian Goat/Ramon Beastdown and Jonathan
Chaos/Roberto Phoenix, both Deck assignments and seats. All four Main Deck
compositions passed the unseen-training gate for both checkpoints. It scored
**27 wins, 36 losses, one draw** in 64 complete experimental-core duels;
its paired-bootstrap score interval was **31.25%–54.69%**. This does not
establish a strength gain. Do not promote either child. The fit on 11/11
training decisions alongside 1/9 held-out transfer and weak match score
supports collecting more varied human judgments and testing generalization
before extending preference optimization.

## Strict reviewed-preference holdout gate (29 October 2026)

`scripts/score_reviewed_preferences.py` now accepts `--require-heldout` to
reject a source replay or seed already used by the scored checkpoint, and
`--require-unseen-main-decks` to reject any Main Deck multiset in its
training provenance. The latter also enforces replay and seed holdout.
Both flags fail closed when the required provenance is missing, and successful
reports record which gates were checked. This makes a fixed-state preference
score usable as a separate held-out diagnostic; it remains distinct from
complete-duel strength.

preferences passed both new holdout gates. The parent ranked the human choice
first at **0/11** and gave it a positive pairwise margin at **0/11**. This
repeats the earlier parent baseline with an explicit gate, not a new model
result. Scoring the 25-preference child on one of its own source replays with
the same gates failed as intended: `review replay is in checkpoint training`.

## On-policy staged Thunder Dragon correction (29 October 2026)

To test whether fresh policy states transfer better than the earlier six-label
synthetic correction, we added an optional `tactical_thunder_search` teacher
and a staged-search focus to `train_behavioral_clone.py`. The teacher uses the
existing Tactical agent with its Thunder search correction; these are
**automated teacher labels, not human approvals**. The two ignored source
batches, `thunder_on_policy_train_124100_124115/` and
`thunder_on_policy_train_124200_124215/`, contain 64 complete native-replay-
verified policy-versus-Tactical games and 32,291 decisions. They yielded 18
staged prompts offering a Thunder Dragon Deck copy; the recorded policy and
teacher disagreed at all 18. The nine recorded zero-copy finishes demonstrate
the recurring error. A two-copy direct choice and the staged `select_card`
path can both be legal ways to take copies, so disagreement is not itself a
proof of bad play at every prompt.

A ten-epoch clone fit on the 18 focused labels without preservation scored
31–33 against its parent in 64 fresh direct duels and 20 wins against Tactical
versus the parent's 24 wins on a matched 64-game schedule. Its saved metadata
incorrectly reports zero teacher disagreements because the aggregate counter
was reset by the focus filter; the counter is fixed in the training script.
This clone was not selected.

A second child fit the same 18 labels with 80 parent-policy KL steps. Its
preservation states came from four complete, replay-verified games generated
by the exact parent checkpoint on the current native assets; the new
`--allow-policy-preservation` option checks checkpoint hash, inference version,
demonstrator seat, replay, and player visibility. It sampled 80 multi-option
preservation states (KL weight 0.1, final reported KL 0.01587). The child
selected a Deck copy at both fresh seed-124001 zero-choice diagnostics. It
scored 36–28 against the parent in 64 direct duels, and 28 wins against
Tactical versus the parent's 27 wins on a matched 64-game schedule. Neither
small result established a reliable strength gain.

A larger prespecified direct check used 256 complete duels on seeds
124700–124731, both seats and Deck assignments, with Theeresak Goat versus
Ramon Beastdown and Christian Goat versus Bryan Chaos. All four Main Deck
compositions were unseen in either checkpoint's training sources. Both agents
used identical v1 own-loss inference. The KL child scored **129 wins, 126
losses, one draw**: score 50.59%, paired-bootstrap 95% interval **46.09%–
55.27%**. This does not establish improvement. Neither child is promoted;
the selected feature-v23 checkpoint and v1 guard remain in use. The result
supports the user's concern that a narrow correction does not solve broader
own-card targeting and timing errors. The next policy experiment should use
reviewed target/activation examples and measure those errors plus match wins
on an independent schedule.

## Idle own-only Ring inference experiment (29 October 2026)

The selected feature-v23 checkpoint is unchanged. An opt-in own-loss guard v3
adds one narrow action filter to v1: on the policy's own turn with no pending
chain, if Ring of Destruction has only the policy's face-up monsters as visible
targets, it defers activation when none has enough current ATK to deal lethal
damage to the opponent. An opposing face-up monster, an ongoing chain, the
opponent's turn, unknown own ATK, and a possible lethal target all retain the
Ring action. The filter sees only the acting player's observation. It is a
strategic experiment, not a legality ruling or a general card-value model.
A [native lethal-own-Ring regression](goat_rules.md#own-monster-ring-can-win)
verifies why the visible lethal exception must remain available.

We compared v3 with the prior v1 guard against Tactical-v14 on four Main Deck
pairings absent from the checkpoint's training games: Theeresak/Phoenix,
Bryan/Mary, Rhymus/Charlotte, and Ramon/Christian. Both deck assignments and
both policy seats were played on two fresh eight-seed blocks, 104000–104007
and 104100–104107. Reports fingerprint the checkpoint, native assets, card
scripts, project source, decks, and schedules. The paired report comparator
verified unseen Main Decks and identical controls within each block.

| Seeds | Games per version | v3 wins | v1 wins | Paired score gain | 95% paired bootstrap interval |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 104000–104007 | 128 | 49 | 47 | +1.56 points | 0 to +3.91 points |
| 104100–104107 | 128 | 53 | 50 | +2.34 points | 0 to +5.47 points |
| Combined | 256 | 102 | 97 | +1.95 points | +0.39 to +3.91 points |

The matched outcome changed in five games, all from a v1 loss to a v3 win;
the other 251 outcomes matched. This is evidence for this narrow schedule,
not a claim that all own-target Rings are bad or that the neural policy
learned to value cards. Both versions still lost most games to Tactical-v14.
Keep v3 experimental until more independent deck and opponent schedules and
reviewed edge cases support promotion. In particular, Ring can be worthwhile
for lethal damage, to respond to removal, or to trigger a monster's effect.

For one changed game, the seed-104000 Theeresak/Phoenix pair with the policy
in seat 1 was re-recorded under both versions. At decision 560 on turn 20,

## One-shot response guard ablation (29 October 2026)

native legality or the neural checkpoint; it does not estimate the value of
all chain responses.

## Residual Ring and MST distillation (29 October 2026)

`visible_residual_guard_distillation_v8` labels only the additional actions
removed by the opt-in combined v5 guard relative to v1. It uses the acting
player's visible observation, offered legal actions, and pinned printed card
Type; the converter verifies each complete native replay and visibility
boundary before writing labels. The trainer recomputes the mask from the
source trajectory and rejects changed labels. These are automated guard
hypotheses, not human reviews or claims about the best surviving move.

The 128 v1-guarded source duels at seeds 104400–104407 produced **56**
comparisons from **22** replays: 47 idle own-only Ring opportunities and

## Expanded own-loss guard held-out strength check (29 October 2026)

The expanded `own_loss_guard` was compared with the *same* selected feature-v23
checkpoint without the guard on four unseen 2005 Main Deck pairings:
Theeresak Goat Control/Phoenix Control, Bryan Chaos/Mary Warrior, Rhymus Goat
Control/Charlotte Zombie, and Ramon Beastdown/Christian Seattle Goat Control.
Both Deck assignments and both policy seats were played on two disjoint
eight-seed blocks, 100500–100507 and 100600–100607. The Main Deck composition
gate rejected an initially proposed Indianapolis pairing already present in
the checkpoint's training set; it was removed before any reported run. Native
assets, scripts, checkpoint, decks, and inference source were fingerprinted.

Directly against the unguarded checkpoint, the guarded version scored
**144–112** over 256 complete duels, or **56.25%** (paired bootstrap 95%
interval **52.34%–60.55%**). The independent seed blocks each scored 72–56.
The pairing splits were 36–28 Beastdown/Seattle Goat, 40–24 Chaos/Warrior,
32–32 Rhymus/Zombie, and 36–28 Theeresak/Phoenix. Against Tactical-v14 on
the exact same schedules, the guarded policy won **95/256** while the
unguarded parent won **81/256**. The strict paired comparator measured a
guarded-minus-parent score gain of **5.47 percentage points** (95% interval
**+2.34 to +8.59 points**); both seed blocks separately had positive paired
intervals. The guarded policy still lost most of its games against Tactical.
These are two fresh seed blocks on four deck families, not a general claim of
superhuman play or a learned neural improvement.

guarded inference mode. Its replay metadata records
`greedy_own_loss_guard_v1`, and its review queue reproduces choices with the

replays remain available for controlled comparisons. The reports are ignored
local artifacts named `own_loss_guard_expanded_direct_*`,

tactical`; use `--both-deck-assignments --require-unseen-main-decks` in all

## Negative-only human review path (29 October 2026)

The local replay viewer now accepts an explicit **Reject the AI's recorded
action** finding. A replay-bound converter validates the saved review and
produces a masked-parent preference that removes only that action's probability
mass. This does not rank the other legal actions or alter game rules. No new
human rejection labels were present in the local review folders at the time of
implementation, so there is **no trained child or measured strength gain**
from this path yet. The previously tested v6 children remain unpromoted.
An end-to-end **synthetic smoke test** used one actual seed-99906 replay frame:
the temporary rejection passed exact native replay and visibility validation,
converted to one negative-only preference, and completed a one-step
masked-parent update with two separate preservation states. The temporary
review and checkpoint were discarded. This verifies the plumbing only; it is
not a human label or evidence of playing strength. The queue UI now counts
saved recorded-action rejections as reviewed and hides them from its default
pending list, while context and upstream notes remain notes.
The training command now rechecks the original queue, saved reviewer note,
source hashes, and any conflicting action choice before accepting a rejection.
Changing a note after conversion invalidates that preference until it is
converted again. A second temporary native-replay smoke test completed one
masked-parent update after this provenance check; its checkpoint was discarded.

## Offline action-branch outcome diagnostic (29 October 2026)

`scripts/evaluate_decision_branches.py` now reconstructs a complete
policy-versus-Tactical duel to one recorded decision, verifies the exact
source replay and player visibility, then plays the recorded action and
specified legal alternatives from the same seed and action prefix. The
recorded-action continuation must reproduce every original decision and the
winner exactly. Both full branch trajectories are independently replay-
verified and visibility-audited. Continuation agents receive only their own
observations and legal actions. The script is an **offline diagnostic**;
sampling the actual hidden state from a recorded game would give an online
search agent forbidden information.

Six observed bad-activation contexts from the v6 training set were branched:
five own-only Nobleman activations and one Breaker activation with only friendly
back row. The alternate action was Pass, Battle Phase, or End Phase, whichever
was offered. **Five of six** pairs ended with the same winner. At seed 99901,
seat 1, decision 424, the original own-target Nobleman line won while the
Battle Phase and End Phase branches lost under these fixed continuation agents.
The position had only the player's own Set D.D. Assailant as a Nobleman target;
this single continuation result does not make that play good. Different
subsequent actions, native random draws, and a single hidden deal can overwhelm
the immediate material loss. It is evidence against treating one branch's
terminal winner as a reliable action label. The ignored report for that pair
has SHA-256 `927831347aa1966134af09f226c9bf10fb486b9e2fc228c5a1e82db6d5395eae`.

Reproduce one early Nobleman comparison with:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m scripts.evaluate_decision_branches \
  .cache/goat-ai/own_card_parent_review_99900_99907/seed_99902_seat_0.json \
  .cache/goat-ai/fv23_current_tactical_broader_33000_33031.pt \
  --decision-index 6 --action-index 3 --action-index 4 \
  --native-root .cache/goat-ai \
  --output-dir .cache/goat-ai/branch_nobleman_99902_6_reproduced
```

The paired reconstruction provides a way to test future value and search
ideas. Before using outcomes for training or online decisions, evaluate
multiple player-consistent hidden-state samples and continuation policies,
then compare their predictions on held-out complete duels. No search agent or
new policy is promoted by this diagnostic.

### Own-Ring target filter ablation (29 October 2026)

An opt-in v4 inference guard extends v3. At a Ring target prompt controlled
by the acting player, it filters nonlethal own face-up targets only when a
face-up opposing monster would deal less damage than the player's current LP.
It preserves an own target that could end the duel and leaves all choices
unchanged if no qualifying opposing target exists. The filter reads only the
acting player's observation and offered legal actions. It does not change the
rules engine or the selected neural checkpoint.

On the previously verified seed-104404 fixed state, v3 selected the player's
own 1900-ATK monster and v4 selected the offered opposing 400-ATK monster.
The rule therefore addresses the reviewed target pattern on that state. A
complete v4-versus-Tactical duel on the same seed and decks reached terminal
in 655 decisions; its replay and visibility audit passed, and
`audit_policy_replays.py` reproduced every v4 policy choice with zero review
flags. Its ignored trajectory is `ring_target_v4_tactical_104404.json` under
`.cache/goat-ai/`.
However, in **128** direct v4-versus-v3 games on fresh seeds 104500–104515,
two unseen-Main-Deck pairings, both deck assignments and both policy seats,
v4 scored **63–65**. A matched v3-versus-v3 control scored **64–64**. The
provenance-checked paired difference was **−0.78 percentage points**, with a
95% interval of **−2.34 to 0.00**. The saved direct report SHA-256 is
`77f1ec49a066e9f02f6443ff073de85058299d53c301f8425f3c43877fa1c9e9`;
the control report SHA-256 is
`c62ef679f44e38373d9f6709fb67aad4c36ff92134eddd2a0a7691445c7660d3`.
Both reports are ignored under `.cache/goat-ai/` with names
`ring_target_v4_vs_v3_104500_104515.json` and
`ring_target_v3_control_104500_104515.json`.

Only one matched game changed its winner. In Mary Triatafilidi Warrior versus
Bryan Coronel Chaos, seed 104513, policy seat 0, v3 won and v4 lost. Complete
duels under both guards were saved, replay-verified, and visibility-audited as
ignored `ring_target_104513_v3.json` and `ring_target_104513_v4.json`. The
first differing decision was **1006**, turn 31 Main Phase 1: v3 selected its

monster, with both players at 5300 LP. The remaining lines diverged. One

## Masked-parent bad-action training pilot (28 October 2026)

The v5 pairwise loss averaged the scores of all alternatives to a flagged
activation. That need not reduce the **total probability** assigned to the
bad action. An opt-in `masked_parent` preference objective now computes the
frozen parent's legal-action distribution at each verified, player-visible
review state, sets the disfavored actions' probability to zero, renormalizes
the remaining actions, and fits the student to that target. This preserves
the parent's relative ranking among the remaining moves. The CLI accepts
this objective only for automated-rule preferences; ordinary human choices
continue to use the existing pairwise objective. Separate current-core
preservation states still receive parent KL.

A pilot started from the unchanged selected feature-v23 checkpoint and used
the **85** `visible_material_avoidance_v5` comparisons in **31** verified
self-play replays from seeds 97000–97063. Four current-core greedy replays on
seeds 99800–99801 supplied **64** separate preservation states. The fit used
20 steps, recorded-bad weight 2, learning rate 0.0001, parent-KL weight 1,
and seed 74. Preference loss fell from **0.8577** to **0.7612**; final sampled
preservation KL was **0.00392**. The ignored checkpoint
`.cache/goat-ai/fv23_masked_parent_97000_97063.pt` has SHA-256
`aa704252322eedc96ae2f3ce38372cc7fa26e2a1c9f67bc521716e0a75fe1be0`.
The v5 labels remain automated tactical hypotheses, not human-reviewed
optimal moves.

On four separate, replay-verified greedy trajectories from seeds 99802–99803,
v5 generated **16** held-out comparisons. The parent ranked a disfavored
action first on **2/16** states and the child on **0/16**. Neither the replay
hashes nor seeds occur in the child's training provenance. These are fixed
states visited by the parent, not complete child games. The ignored parent
and child score reports have SHA-256
`30ef66c1162e409b7eb8e67b82fe735c1d98768065d7d941f1359ab083c87293`
and `9431111f8adb3bbb5bfe1b19982e97a1b4edbf4c98dea2e05ae1b393eb33507a`.

On unseen Phoenix/Dimension Fusion and Ryan Hayakawa/Bryan Coronel Main Deck

### Full-choice Ring branch diagnostic (29 October 2026)

A flagged own-only Ring of Destruction decision in the verified
`ring_guard_blind_104400_104407/matchup_01_seed_104406_seat_0.json` replay
was branched at zero-based decision **89**. The selected v23 policy activated
Ring on turn 3 at 8000–8000 LP, then targeted its own 1900-ATK monster;
that recorded branch lost. Reconstructing the exact seed and action prefix,
then continuing with the same v23 policy and Tactical-v14 opponent, produced
these terminal outcomes:

| Initial action | Policy-seat outcome | Verified decisions |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Activate Ring (recorded action index 4) | Loss | 670 |
| Enter Battle Phase (index 5) | Loss | 561 |
| Enter End Phase (index 6) | Win | 468 |

The recorded-action branch reproduced the source replay exactly. All three
complete branches passed native replay and player-visibility verification.
The ignored report is
`.cache/goat-ai/ring_full_choice_branch_104406_d89/report.json` (SHA-256
`bf7484d1ece96d5ce1b30738cb99c407e42bc8c1b64837e1f41a88bf9c885e8f`);
its branch trajectory SHA-256 values are recorded there. Reproduce with
`scripts/evaluate_decision_branches.py` using the source replay, selected
`fv23_current_tactical_broader_33000_33031.pt` checkpoint, `--decision-index
89 --action-index 4 --action-index 5 --action-index 6` and an empty output
directory. This is an offline, full-state, single-seed diagnostic: its win
reversal does not establish expected action value or an online search method.
It does show why a target-only correction is insufficient. The avoidable
choice was activating Ring; the better tested branch held it and ended the
turn.

A batch of the same offline test covered all **13** flagged own-only Ring
activations in the 128-duel audit where `end_phase` was legal; one other flag
had no End Phase option and was excluded. Of the 13 paired continuations,
**nine lost in both branches, three won in both, and one changed from a loss
after activation to a win after End Phase**. No case changed from a win to a
loss, but these are selected, correlated decision states, not independent
games or an estimate of how often a revised policy would win. The continuations
reuse the same policy, which may make later mistakes even after deferring Ring.
Each recorded branch reproduced its source, and all 26 branches passed exact
native replay and visibility checks. The ignored batch summary is
`.cache/goat-ai/ring_flagged_end_phase_repro_104400_104407/summary.json`
(SHA-256 `4502f04da7e7dfcd4ea3ea7ef8cdf02dc7e5372a914057f78ca30a0d6d363670`).
Regenerate it with:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src:. OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 .venv/bin/python \
  scripts/evaluate_flagged_phase_branches.py \
  .cache/goat-ai/ring_guard_blind_104400_104407/audit_upstream_128.json \
  .cache/goat-ai/fv23_current_tactical_broader_33000_33031.pt \
  --native-root .cache/goat-ai --category ring_idle_only_own_faceup \
  --phase-action end_phase --output-dir .cache/goat-ai/NEW_EMPTY_DIRECTORY
```

The experimental residual-v8 child ranks Ring below another action in all
**14** flagged states, but every source replay is in that child's training
provenance. Its top alternatives are Battle Phase in ten cases, Normal Summon
in three, and Set a Spell/Trap in one; it does not necessarily learn to hold
Ring until a good target appears. At decision 89 above, the child chooses a
Normal Summon. Using that child for both the branch action and subsequent
policy decisions wins the continuation, whereas forcing the recorded Ring
activation before continuing with the same child loses. Both branches passed
replay and visibility verification. The ignored report is
`.cache/goat-ai/ring_v8_child_branch_104406_d89/report.json` (SHA-256
`01bfb8bfdcc5032a31ea834e6e82062b47212691bebd131a92f9e49deff3ef73`).
`scripts/evaluate_decision_branches.py --continuation-checkpoint` now supports
this paired changed-policy diagnostic. This trained-state example does not
establish generalization; the earlier fresh 64-duel direct comparison remains
**31–33** for the child against its parent.

schedule trained Jesse Twohig Indianapolis Goat Control/Montague Warrior
and DingoSig Chaos Return/Weirdchamp Bazoo Return. The rollout used four
parallel native workers, four-game frozen PPO batches, two epochs, batch
size 32, per-episode weighting, frozen-rollout learner-deck baseline,
learning rate 0.00005, parent KL weight 0.5, and a 50% frozen historical-
snapshot probability with Tactical-v14 otherwise. Independent opponent RNG
was enabled. All 128 games reached terminal state: **48 wins, 79 losses,

### Retaining own-loss preferences during PPO (29 October 2026)

The self-play trainer now optionally revalidates the 49 native-replayed V11
source trajectories and their 55 automated selected-mistake preferences against
the starting checkpoint's file hashes. During PPO, a small auxiliary KL term
keeps the policy near its starting distribution after the recorded bad actions
are masked out. It uses only the recorded acting player's observation. This is
an experimental training signal, not a rule that prohibits self-targeting;
some self-targeting plays are correct. The manifest hash is
`dea6e23d04534b115f76135ac080c87dd41068a46f0a019f26cc7939ff576aa2`.

Two children started from the same V11 checkpoint and played the same 128
training seeds, 106800–106927, against the same mixed Tactical and historical
snapshot pool. Both used clipped PPO, a 0.5 parent KL weight, and the same
optimizer and rollout schedule. The retention arm additionally used preference
weight 0.1 and eight anchors per PPO minibatch. Their first four replay hashes
matched exactly before the first update. Both runs reached 128 terminal games
without a decision cap or unsupported game. The retention run took **87.03 s**
and the control **40.03 s** on this machine. These are training wall times, not
simulator throughput benchmarks. The retained checkpoint SHA-256 is
`bc57217f0ba7c7e7316a02f6c06651469cf5c48d46080326aef709dc38e5d054`;
the control SHA-256 is
`ba46349d86cd4761cb03dd78bad7fef8fd20ee91c5242d8681f938b3bd625975`.

On 26 untouched verified own-loss decisions, the control ranked a recorded bad
action first **2/26** times and retention **1/26**. On five untouched Ring/MST
decisions, the counts were **2/5** and **1/5**. These fixed-state checks show a
small reduction on sampled mistakes; they do not estimate fresh in-game error
frequency. The retention arm's 128 saved training trajectories passed native
replay and visibility audit.

For full-game evaluation, both children used the 2005 Nationals Max Suffridge
and Jonathan Labounty Main Decks, plus the Theeresak Poonsombat Seattle list;
the exact Main Deck compositions were absent from training. Both deck orders
and policy seats were tested. Retention scored **32–32** directly against the
matched control on seeds 107000–107007. Against Tactical-v14 on separate
matched seeds 107008–107015, **both scored 16–48**. The paired retention-minus-
control Tactical score difference was **0 percentage points**, with a 95%
paired bootstrap interval of **−9.4 to +9.4 points**. The report comparator
verified equal native assets, scripts, source, schedules, and unseen Main Decks.
These results do not establish a competitive improvement, and the added
training cost is substantial. Keep both PPO children experimental and retain
the v23 selected checkpoint. The ignored reports and trajectories are under
`.cache/goat-ai/v11_ppo_retention_heldout_107000_107015/` and
`.cache/goat-ai/fv23_v11_ppo_{retain,control}_128_106800_106927*`.

Eight new greedy complete duels per child were then recorded against
Tactical-v14 on seeds 107100–107101 with both policy seats and two Nationals
Main Deck pairings. All **16** reached terminal state and passed native replay,
visibility, and saved-policy choice verification. The same conservative own-
card audit flagged **three** activation decisions for each child: two early
MST uses with only own back row visible, and one Nobleman activation with only
an own Set monster. The retained child had one additional flagged target
prompt for MST against a resolving one-shot Spell/Trap; that prompt offered
only one legal target, so the optional MST activation is the decision needing
review. The audit's activation counts were 2/2 available MST situations and
1/1 available Nobleman situations for **both** children. These counts describe
this small visited-state sample, not a population mistake rate. They show the
fixed-state preference gain did not generalize to these repeated positions.
The replay/audit files are in the ignored directory
`.cache/goat-ai/v11_ppo_retention_fresh_107100_107101/`.

The V11 preference generator labels selected Nobleman own-loss activations but
does not currently label an idle own-only MST activation. This is a concrete
coverage gap. Future training should expand *verified, player-visible*
activation comparisons across more decks and contexts, distinguish optional
activation from forced target prompts, and reserve fresh seeds for testing
generalization. Neither a simple card-count heuristic nor these few labels
establishes whether a play is strategically good in every position.

### V12 own-MST preference trial (29 October 2026)

`visible_selected_own_loss_with_own_mst_v12` adds a narrow automated
comparison to V11: when the recorded policy chooses MST and the only other
back row card is its own face-up printed Normal/Quick-Play Spell or Normal
Trap, prefer an actually offered pass. The rule skips Set cards, other
visible back row, forced target prompts, and positions without a pass. It is
an experimental training label, not a legality restriction or a universal
claim about using MST on one's own card. The parser and trainer validate its
rule-set ID and recompute the label from the player-visible replay.

The V12 generator native-replayed and visibility-audited all 128 control PPO
training trajectories from seeds 106800–106927. It wrote **34 selected-error
comparisons from 30 replays**, including **three** new own-face-up-MST cases.
The ignored manifest SHA-256 is
`2b410cb3d76e817c3f99cae6ddb1f54b6023b4e538f8c7313f04fff47043faba`.
An experimental 40-step child of V11 used these 34 comparisons, four separate
current-core preservation trajectories (64 states), masked-parent objective,
recorded-bad weight 10, parent KL weight 1, learning rate 0.0001, and seed 83.
Its preference loss fell **1.1317 → 0.8977**; final sampled preservation KL
was **0.01356**. Checkpoint SHA-256:
`82e707470ffbf9e0f8a50e36cf377597d358a5d7b55b0064dd5085325ee157a9`.

The preservation trajectories included the Theeresak Seattle deck. The
unseen-Main-Deck gate correctly rejected a first proposed comparison that
included it. The valid comparison used only the Max Suffridge and Jonathan
Labounty 2005 Nationals Main Decks, both deck orders and both policy seats.
On new seeds 107320–107335, V12 scored **30–34** directly against V11. On
matched seeds 107336–107351 against Tactical-v14, V12 scored **14–50** and V11
**21–43**. The paired V12-minus-V11 Tactical score difference was **−10.9
percentage points**, 95% paired bootstrap interval **−21.9 to −1.6 points**.
The report comparator verified equal assets, scripts, source, schedule, and
unseen Main Decks. This trial did not improve full-game strength. The small
MST label addition is entangled with 31 other selected-error comparisons, so
the match difference cannot be attributed to MST labels alone. Keep V12
experimental; the selected v23 checkpoint remains unchanged. Ignored reports
are under `.cache/goat-ai/v12_heldout_107320_107351/`.

The policy input already contains separate own and opposing back-row counts,
and `select_card` actions carry relative controller and field slot. Thus the
ownership distinction is representable, although the policy may still learn
a broad MST action bias. To probe that question, we scored the replay-verified
seed-107100 opening at decision 6 (MST versus pass) under V11 and V12. V11

Changing only the visible Swords controller to the opponent in an offline

fell by about seven points. This single synthetic observation is **not** a
native-verified alternate duel or strength estimate; it suggests the child

Four additional greedy complete duels per checkpoint on untouched seeds

activation. The cases differ, and four games per arm cannot establish a
mistake-rate difference. Ignored trajectories and audits are under
`.cache/goat-ai/v12_fresh_107400_107401/`. A stronger next experiment needs
many varied, verified ownership contexts and separate positive examples of
valuable removal; the fixed-state target should be paired with fresh-game
error and competitive results before any policy promotion.

and **12 mixed** visible back-row contexts. The matched preference-retention
arm had **11**, **10**, and **13**, respectively. Only two control and one
retention opposing-only choices faced exactly one visible face-up opposing
back-row card; most of the possible positive examples involve Set cards or

not legal-opportunity counts or good/bad-play rates. Both sets of 128

Ignored catalog SHA-256 values are
`7fa49cf13f19f526412ebb4772f313a9c40b93d704699fdd3bbcae6d9b155ef4`
and
`45b3c661b6f57d124bf267611d921c9645cc4c4e1fbfbfbbab36f2a994947f63`.

## Visible own-card losses in the selected policy (28 October 2026)

### Observed material at shortlisted own-card decisions (29 October 2026)

The 17 decisions in the outcome-blind [own-card review queue](replay_audit.md#idle-own-ring-coverage-and-outcome-blind-review-29-october-2026)
were checked again against their exact native replays and player-visibility
audit: **10,659** source decisions verified. For the **15** selected effect
activations with a later decision after the chain closed, the acting player's
visible hand-plus-non-Token-field margin changed by **−1** in one case,
**−2** in eleven, and **−3** in three. One of the other queue decisions is a
later Ring target prompt, not an activation. The remaining Ring activation
ended the duel with an open chain, so no post-chain material result is
reported for it. None of the 15 measured intervals included another
selected activation.

This quantifies the recorded material losses in a selected set of suspicious
plays. It does not estimate the value of an alternative action, hidden
responses, effect synergies, or how often the same mistakes occur in fresh
games. The ignored report is
`.cache/goat-ai/ring_guard_blind_104400_104407/observed_material_at_review_v1.json`
(SHA-256 `ba327e75daa7a5ca2e281c8346ade7149e98c53f3f26f96c703ddb1cbe48e7dd`).
Reproduce it with:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src:. .venv/bin/python scripts/audit_review_material.py \
  .cache/goat-ai/ring_guard_blind_104400_104407/own_card_review_queue.json \
  --native-root .cache/goat-ai \
  --output .cache/goat-ai/ring_guard_blind_104400_104407/observed_material_at_review_v1.json
```

The model already encodes the target's controller and public board counts,
but those inputs have not produced reliable avoidance of these losses. The
next checkpoint comparison should measure own-card activation and target
errors at their *opportunities* in fresh complete games, alongside match
strength, rather than treating total decision count as the denominator.

The weak average material association and the v5 preference trial do **not**
show that visibly wasteful self-targeting is rare or harmless. A focused audit
used 64 sampled, replay-verified and visibility-audited self-play trajectories
on seeds 90300–90363 (24,851 total decisions). The recorded learner made seven
own-only Nobleman of Crossout activations, four Heavy Storm activations with
only its own back row present, and one Breaker effect targeting its own back
row with no opposing back row. The audit also found three Heavy Storm choices
whose visible back-row trade was nonpositive, two Tribe-Infecting Virus
activations with no visible enemy monster, and two Tribe Type choices that hit
only friendly monsters. These are **review flags**, not proof that every
activation was strategically wrong; a deliberate self-destruction line can
sometimes have value.

At those flagged states, the frozen selected v23 checkpoint's greedy choice
reproduced the same category of own-card loss on **5/7** Nobleman, **3/4**
own-only Heavy Storm, and **1/1** Breaker prompts. This is a fixed-state
comparison on states visited by a sampled policy, not a fresh greedy rollout
or an estimate of how often greedy play reaches them. It nevertheless shows
the failure survives in the selected policy. The earlier v5 preference fit
covered own-only Nobleman and negative Heavy Storm, plus boss self-banish and
Tribe Type choices. It did not train a general self-target decision rule or
establish a strength gain, so the selected checkpoint remains unchanged.

Reproduce with `scripts/audit_policy_replays.py` on
`.cache/goat-ai/ppo_independent_mixed_90300_90363_replays/episode_*.json`,
using `--checkpoint .cache/goat-ai/fv23_current_tactical_broader_33000_33031.pt
--compare-parent-greedy --native-root .cache/goat-ai`. The ignored audit JSON
has SHA-256
`444fe4b1f748119bbd104f7ec8c1663fa8b9e00f9159cc95bd8ab60ac94270ca`.
The next learning experiment should measure activation **and** target/Type
selection separately for own-card removal, then validate improved mistake
rates and match results on fresh games. It should compare pass/hold options
before activation, because choosing a less harmful target after an unnecessary
activation cannot recover the spent card.

`scripts/audit_policy_replays.py` now includes a
`visible_own_card_losses` aggregate for greedy policy evaluation replays. It
uses reproduced policy choices as the denominator and counts the conservative
own-card review categories, which are deduplicated per category, turn, and
phase. For own-only Nobleman and Heavy Storm it also counts distinct visited
turn/phase states where activation was legal, so their selection rates have
an opportunity denominator. Sampled self-play reports deliberately do not
get a greedy rate.

As a fresh current-core baseline, the selected v23 policy played Tactical-v14
in eight terminal duels on seeds 99800–99803, alternating policy seats across
the Theeresak/Christian Seattle and Rhymus/Dimension Fusion matchups. All
eight trajectories passed exact native replay verification and visibility
auditing; all **2,398** policy decisions were reproduced from the checkpoint.
The aggregate found **three** flagged own-card losses: two own-only Nobleman
activations and one Heavy Storm that hit only its own back row, or **1.25
flagged instances per 1,000 policy decisions**. Among visited distinct
turn/phase opportunities, own-only Nobleman was offered **6** times and
selected **2** times; own-only Heavy Storm was offered **8** times and selected
**1** time. Four games per matchup and category/turn/phase deduplication make
this a baseline diagnostic, not a population error-rate estimate. Other
categories may simply not have arisen. The ignored replay directory is
`.cache/goat-ai/fresh_self_loss_99800_99803/`; its audit JSON has SHA-256
`66700d1e91507a453ad5bf3776a33651e3cebf4211b57694c63612da6864c1e0`.
Run `scripts/record_policy_match.py` with the selected checkpoint, the named
decks, seeds, and seats, then `scripts/audit_policy_replays.py` with that
checkpoint and the eight generated JSON files to reproduce the report.

## Broader-deck human-review preference pilot (28 October 2026)

### Reviewed material-direction check (29 October 2026)

The earlier New Jersey and broader-deck review manifests contain **25 changed
human choices** in total (14 and 11). Their review-bound preference files were
read against the exact source trajectories; the four distinct duels relevant
to this check were replay-verified and visibility-audited again. Five changed
choices preferred Heavy Storm when its *visible, before-chain* card-count
margin was **+1**: the opponent had two or three back-row cards, and the
reviewed player had either a Set Heavy Storm plus zero or one other back-row
card, or Heavy Storm in hand with no own back row. One changed choice rejected
Nobleman of Crossout when the only visible Set monster belonged to the acting
player and no opposing Set monster existed. These six directions agree with a
simple local material count; actual value may still depend on hidden cards,
chains, effects, and future turns. They are not six independent games or a
validated reward function. None of the 25 changed human choices was an MST
activation, so the new [MST opportunity queue](replay_audit.md#mst-use-and-non-use-review-queue-29-october-2026)
addresses a current review-data gap rather than repeating existing labels.

As an independent diagnostic, `scripts/score_reviewed_preferences.py`
replayed and visibility-checked all 13 source trajectories containing these
25 changed preferences, then scored the selected v23 parent and the earlier
feature-v25 visible-trade head. None of the source seeds occurred in either
checkpoint's training provenance. V25 ranked a reviewed alternative first in
**3/25** decisions versus **0/25** for the parent; all three were among the

(mean **619.25**). The action counter recorded **34 selected Scapegoat chain
responses** and **33 selected Metamorphosis activations**; Thousand-Eyes
Restrict appeared in selected field actions. Thus the sweep exercised the
intended interaction rather than only including those cards in Deck lists.

## Selected-policy Thunder Dragon training-label audit (28 October 2026)

The selected feature-v23 checkpoint records SHA-256 provenance for 144

19 times and took zero six times; Tactical-v7 supplied none of these prompts.

rerun native replay verification or establish that every two-copy choice was

## Fixed-policy visible-margin outcome diagnostic (27 October 2026)

The same 64 frozen-checkpoint, native-verified policy-versus-Tactical duels
used for the [critic check](#fixed-policy-visible-state-critic-check-27-october-2026)
also test the user's card-advantage hypothesis without a policy-change
confound. At the first policy-seat Main Phase 1 of turn 4 in each duel, one
player-visible snapshot counted hand and field cards, excluding Sheep Tokens,
and compared that margin with the eventual binary outcome. It also recorded
the visible Life Point margin. Each duel contributes one sample, including
both deck pairings and policy seats; the policy won 18/64 games. The saved
summary checks all snapshot hashes against the collector manifest. The
separate critic comparison had already independently replay-verified the
same 31,729 decisions and reproduced the checkpoint's 15,704 choices.

Overall win-versus-loss ranking AUC was **0.561** for visible card count and
**0.671** for Life Point margin. Resampling whole four-game seeds 10,000
times gave 95% intervals **0.370–0.759** for card count and **0.505–0.830**
for Life Points. The paired LP-minus-card AUC interval was **−0.203 to
+0.402**; this small corpus does not establish that either margin is better.
By pairing, card-count AUC was **0.514** for Jesse Goat Control/Warrior and
**0.628** for Phoenix/Dimension Fusion; LP AUC was **0.668** and **0.742**.
Card count alone is a weak and uncertain early predictor here. Later-turn
snapshots are conditional on duels lasting that long and can reflect the
consequence of winning, so this retrospective audit does not identify an
action's causal value or justify a shaped reward. It also omits card quality,
hidden holdings, and future draws.

The ignored raw audit SHA-256 is
`cdc560e583c1cfb6fcd5ad210bd220c591a4554677ca033d624104854866b92b`;
the ignored summary SHA-256 is
`5af727ea547662c7a2af809361d0052ea8ea7409bb10e7999aac6127cf6e068d`.

played Tactical-v14 on two deck pairings: Jesse Goat Control versus Warrior,
and 2005 Phoenix Control versus WikiFormat Dimension Fusion. Seeds
44000–44015 covered both policy seats for each pairing, producing **64
complete duels and 31,729 native replay-verified, visibility-audited
decisions**. The critic comparison independently verified every trajectory
and reproduced **15,704 recorded policy choices** against the unchanged
checkpoint. The collector manifest SHA-256 is
`93c2f2f5f768b912b76d9033408f833a1eef972a6d1371021f6a3287b72fffa6`.

The first 12 whole seeds supplied 48 training duels with 768 evenly spaced
multi-option policy-seat decisions; the final four whole seeds supplied 16
holdout duels with 256 such decisions. Each split has both pairings and seats.
The critics each used width 32, two epochs, learning rate 0.001, and the same
initial seed 171. Targets were the learner's terminal win/loss outcome; a
constant predictor used the training games' mean return. On the holdout,
per-game mean squared error was **0.866** for the constant, **1.151** for v1,

first pairing had 2/8 policy wins on holdout; the second had 3/8. This is a
value-prediction diagnostic, not a policy-strength result. These critics do
not justify changing the default PPO baseline on this fixed-policy evidence.
Training on more diverse fixed-policy games or a different value objective
remains open; repeated tuning against these 16 holdout games would invalidate
their use as an untouched check.

and policy seats, seeds 47400–47403. The frozen checkpoint is the same in all
80 duels. All **39,552 decisions** were native replay-verified and visibility
audited for this comparison; 768, 256, and 256 multi-option policy-seat
decisions were sampled from training, holdout, and independent games.

With width 32, two epochs, learning rate `0.001`, and seed 171, per-game
outcome MSE was:

| Predictor | Held-out seeds | Independent decks |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Constant training-return mean | 0.866 | 0.866 |
| v1 visible-state critic | 1.151 | 1.150 |
| v2 visible-state critic | 1.169 | 1.187 |

The v2-minus-v1 paired bootstrap 95% interval was **−0.005 to +0.055** on
held-out seeds and **+0.001 to +0.078** on independent decks. Both fitted
critics underperform the constant baseline on these data. The independent
deck result supports v1 over v2 for this specific fit, but neither critic
has earned use as a PPO baseline. This experiment used one training seed and
only 16 independent games; it is a prediction diagnostic, not a measured
policy-strength change.

## Fixed-policy resource regression check (27 October 2026)

The earlier six-input resource network underfit on the shared two-epoch Adam
schedule. A separate closed-form ridge regression now uses the same six
player-visible differences: Life Points, hand count, monster count, backrow
count, Deck count, and turn. Each duel has equal total weight regardless of
its number of sampled decisions. The six inputs are standardized using only
training games, the intercept is unpenalized, and the fixed coefficient
penalty is `0.1` per training game. Predictions are clipped to the legal
terminal-return range of −1 to +1. No hidden identities, future outcome, or
opponent Deck order enter a prediction.

The frozen feature-v23 policy supplied 48 training duels (seeds 44000–44011)
and 16 held-out duels (44012–44015) from the prior corpus. A new
16-duel transfer check used the Guide Dimension Fusion Turbo and Rhymus Lizo
Goat Control decks in both assignments and policy seats, seeds 48100–48103.
Both Main Deck compositions are absent from the policy checkpoint's
training games. The new collection recorded **7,402 decisions**. The
comparison independently native replay-verified and visibility-audited all
**39,131 decisions** across 80 duels, and sampled 768 training, 256 held-out,
and 256 transfer decisions with multiple legal actions.

| Predictor | Held-out seed MSE | New pairing MSE |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Constant training-return mean | 0.866 | 0.637 |
| v1 embedding critic | 1.151 | 0.698 |
| v2 embedding critic | 1.169 | 0.705 |
| Two-epoch resource network | 1.309 | 1.412 |
| Closed-form resource ridge | **0.692** | **0.572** |

The ridge-minus-constant paired bootstrap 95% interval was **−0.424 to
+0.056** on held-out seeds and **−0.292 to +0.099** on the new pairing.
The point estimates favor the ridge baseline, but both intervals include
zero. This is a retrospective outcome-prediction diagnostic on only 16 games
per check, not evidence of a stronger playing policy or of causal value for
the six features. Keep the current self-play baseline unchanged; an opt-in
ridge-baseline ablation needs a larger independent schedule and held-out
competitive matches before promotion.

## Frozen mirror self-play value transfer (27 October 2026)

The policy recorder now supports `--opponent mirror_policy`: it loads the same
frozen checkpoint independently for each seat and records the opponent
checkpoint hash. This makes a deterministic self-play value diagnostic without
PPO changing the policy during data collection. With both `--policy-seat`
values on each seed/deck assignment, a physical duel is recorded twice, once
for each player's outcome perspective. These are **not independent duels**;
uncertainty below resamples whole seed blocks, keeping both assignments and
perspectives together. All replays were native verified and visibility audited.

First, the six-resource ridge fitted on policy-versus-Tactical games above
was tested on **16 mirror records** (eight distinct duels) from Phoenix
Control versus Guide Dimension Fusion Turbo, both assignments, seeds
48200–48203. It scored **1.071** per-game outcome MSE. The Tactical-trained
constant scored 1.210, but a zero-return mirror baseline scored **1.000**.
The ridge-minus-zero seed-clustered bootstrap 95% interval was **+0.003 to
+0.141**. This fit does not justify use in self-play PPO.

A separate ridge was then fitted on **96 mirror records** from 2005 Rhymus
Goat Control versus Charlotte Zombie, both assignments and perspectives,
seeds 48300–48323. The remaining **32 records**, seeds 48324–48331, were
held out; the Phoenix/Dimension 16 records supplied a different-deck check.
The 128 Rhymus/Zombie records contain 64 distinct frozen-policy duels and
**68,840** decisions. The final comparison independently replay-verified and
visibility-audited **77,124** decisions across all 144 records. The ridge
uses only six acting-player-visible resource differences, equal total weight
per recorded perspective, fixed L2 shrinkage, and no hidden card identities.

| Predictor | Held-out Rhymus/Zombie MSE | Phoenix/Dimension MSE |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Zero-return mirror baseline | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| v1 embedding critic, two epochs | 0.895 | 1.342 |
| v2 embedding critic, two epochs | 0.895 | 2.050 |
| Resource network, two epochs | 1.089 | 1.083 |
| Self-play-trained resource ridge | **0.727** | **0.790** |

Ridge-minus-zero 95% intervals from whole-seed bootstrap were **−0.394 to
−0.122** on eight held-out seeds and **−0.292 to −0.067** on four
different-deck seeds. The point estimate and interval favor this small
value model on these fixed-policy trajectories, but the different-deck check
has only four seed blocks. Outcome prediction is not a measured improvement
in decisions or competitive strength. The selected policy and PPO baseline
remain unchanged pending a controlled PPO ablation and held-out matches.
